mentl/e903cd7:
BinOp Concat in the lowerer defaulted to list_concat whenever both
operand types were still TVars at lower time. Inside a polymorphic
body — e.g. `fn cat(a, b) = a ++ sep ++ b` passed as an argument to
fold — the types ARE still TVars when the body is lowered, because
the lowerer sees them before the outer call site's unification
resolves them. So every polymorphic concat got list_concat regardless
of what it would eventually be concatenating.

Changed the fallback to val_concat (which dispatches at runtime via
a byte-pattern heuristic — correct behavior for "types genuinely
aren't known at lower time"). The existing concrete dispatch for
TString and TList is unchanged.

## Definitive answer for the multi-line lex bug

The bootstrap's `Parse error [1:20]: expected Eq got Eof` on
`let a = 1\nlet b = 2` was NOT a lexer bug. Primitives all checked
out (read_stdin, chars, byte_at, is_whitespace, ch == "\n", str_eq).
The actual failure was upstream: in `compile_wasm`, `strip_imports`
does `source |> split("\n") |> filter_non_imports(0) |> join("\n")`,
and `join` uses fold with `|acc, x| acc ++ sep ++ x`. That polymorphic
lambda was being compiled to list_concat by the lowerer. The split/
join roundtrip corrupted the user source by treating string fragments
as lists. lex then received the corrupted bytes.

Instrumented both lex_from and build_chars inside a rebuilt bootstrap
and read the trace — at pos 9 the lexer saw byte=9 (not 10), pos 10/
11/12 saw 0, and pos 13 saw 'l'. The 5 bytes `09 00 00 00 6c` are the
LAYOUT of a 5-byte char chunk whose length is 9 and whose payload is
'l' — meaning the "next allocation" after the source was another
9-byte string. The source had been stored as TWO separate strings
whose concatenation was broken, not one 19-byte string.

## Verification via Rust VM

  fn a3(xs, sep) = { fn cat(a,b) = a++sep++b; fold(xs,"a",cat) };
  a3(["b","c"], "-")
    before → "a \x01\x00\x00 -"
    after  → "a-b-c"

  all 4 crucibles still pass
